A lot of questions this week on funding, so here's how a GPU typically gets funded at $IREN.

First, the customer signs a multi-year take-or-pay contract and agrees to a prepayment. On our recent 3-year contracts, prepayments have been 45% to 55% of the associated GPU capex.

Second, financing is committed, secured by the contracted GPUs. On the Microsoft contract we secured an A-rated facility at around 6%, which together with prepayments covers 96% of GPU capex. More recently, for a non-investment grade counterparty at Mackenzie, we secured financing at 9% fixed, which together with prepayments covers more than the full cost of the GPUs.

That's the GPU side. The data centers are a separate, long-term asset base, and we own the ones our GPUs run in. Construction has been funded from cash to date, with no debt against these multi-billion dollar assets. As they come online with contracted customers, they can support financing in their own right.

The processes behind the next facilities are continuing, and new paper will cost what the market charges. With GPU paybacks of around two years on our recent 3-year contracts, a wider spread barely moves the economics.

There's more customer demand than we can build for. posts.text:
Each of the last several decades had a clear winner, an asset that rose so far and so persistently that it came to seem like the obvious place for money.
Each went on to disappoint in the decade that followed.

The pattern is consistent across very different assets: 
* Gold rose more than thirteen-fold in the inflationary 1970s, then lost ground through the 1980s as inflation fell. 
* Japanese stocks rose nearly six-fold in the 1980s, then lost half their value in the 1990s, beginning a slump that lasted decades. 
* The Nasdaq rose roughly nine-fold in the 1990s, then fell 44 percent in the 2000s. 
* Emerging market stocks nearly tripled in the 2000s, then barely moved in the 2010s.

In each case, the decade’s winner ended it with the widest following, the most confident forecasts, and the highest prices relative to its fundamentals.

posts.text:
The Production Principle will change your life.

Technology dominates our life. Everywhere you turn there is a television, a computer, and a mobile phone. In modern society, it is hard to do anything without being inundated with algorithms and screens. Many people are worried about the effect these new technologies will have on us over the long-run.

Most parents try not to give their children computers or phones. Others do their best to limit their screen time. And adults are no better off. There is a growing body of research that suggests people are becoming addicted to their electronic devices at an unprecedented rate.

But the problem with shutting off these devices and avoiding them all together is you will lose access to information and productivity. It is undeniable how helpful computers, phones, and other devices can be for anyone with curiosity and capacity for work.

So what is the balance? How do you get the benefit of technology devices without being imprisoned by their negative side-effects?

Venture capitalist @KTmBoyle has the best answer — she calls it The Production Principle. Here is how Katherine describes the principle:

"My rule for tech is simple, one I call The Production Principle: “Produce more than you consume.” It’s easy to measure and remember. And it’s the rule guiding tech usage in our house for everyone, child or adult.

If kids are sitting on their phones scrolling social media and consuming memes and slop without your knowledge, that’s not good and probably not very healthy. But if they’re making things, coding, interacting with videos that teach them to build things online and off, that’s generally a positive thing, especially if you’re engaged in these activities with them as a parent.

Computers and screens govern so many fields today. By the time my children are teenagers, I imagine screens and code will govern much, much more of the world around us. I don’t plan to hide this from them because I don’t want them to be afraid of the modern world, or to sense that they can’t control their relationship to it.

Instilling the Production Principle early changes their relationship with technology. It becomes theirs to master, not a nebulous thing to fear."

This principle is great because it focuses on what you are doing with technology, rather than forcing technology to be classified in a binary good or bad designation. The truth is technology can be both. It really depends on how you use it, which is why The Production Principle forces you to be productive or to put down your device.

Once I started implementing The Production Principle, my screen time decreased and my productivity increased. Double win. Now I try my best to use technology for what it was originally intended…being more efficient and productive.

And it never hurts to have accountability partners. I have relied on @polinapompliano to constantly ask me, “Are you being productive or are you wasting time?” whenever I am on my phone. I do the same thing with her. Together we have done a great job of overcoming the perils of technology, while leveraging the great advancements to our advantage.

Stay vigilant about how you use devices moving forward. The Production Principle works.

This is an excerpt from my new book, How To Live An Extraordinary Life Volume 2. You can buy a copy of the book here: https://www.amazon.com/How-Live-Extraordinary-Life-Two/dp/1804094153/

Q4 and post-midterm seasonality remain overwhelmingly bullish.
Historically, the fourth quarter has been the strongest quarter of the year for the S&P 500 in terms of consistency of positive returns. Over roughly the past 80 years, Q4 has produced a positive return about 80% of the time, compared with approximately 60%–64% for the other three quarters.
The midterm election cycle adds another powerful seasonal tailwind. Stocks have historically performed particularly well as the uncertainty surrounding midterm elections is removed. Depending on the precise starting period used, recent historical studies put the S&P 500's positive rate during Q4 of midterm years at roughly 83%–85%. 
Given the backdrop of strong earnings growth and, at least for now, no clear evidence of recession, history argues that the bulls should continue to receive the benefit of the doubt.
However, seasonality is a tendency—not a guarantee. Fed tightening, deteriorating breadth, rising interest rates and elevated oil prices represent meaningful counterweights. At a minimum, those conditions increase the probability of volatility and make the current environment considerably less straightforward than the historical averages suggest. 
Individual stocks have already been correcting beneath the surface of the major indexes. More than 35% of S&P 500 stocks are currently down 20% or more from their 52-week highs, even as the index itself remains relatively close to record territory. In other words, a significant correction has already occurred—it has simply been masked by the strength of a relatively small number of heavily weighted stocks.
Interestingly, the 87 Crash  is one of the historical analogs worth keeping in mind following a Fed tightening. The comparison should not be interpreted as a prediction of another crash, but the monetary-policy parallel is real: the Fed raised the discount rate from 5.5% to 6.0% on September 4, 1987, while market interest rates were already rising sharply. 
The seasonal winds are clearly at the market's back. The question is whether tightening financial conditions, weak participation and rising oil become strong enough headwinds to overpower them.

I don't know if you realize what just happened.

Elon Musk is completely bypassing the State.

For 100 years, we've been told the problem is capital. That it must be captured, taxed, redistributed. With an army of intermediaries standing between those who create wealth and the people: ministries, agencies, commissions, bureaucrats.

Musk is doing the opposite. He's taking his capital and giving it directly to the people. One SpaceX share to every kid in America. Not a handout. Not a subsidy. A piece of the machine that's taking humanity to Mars.

And he says it himself: this is the first of many.

Mises understood this back in 1944: the bureaucrat creates nothing. He administers what others created, following rules that have no connection to the value produced. The day value flows directly from the one who creates it to the one who receives it, the bureaucrat has no function left.

That's what's being born right now. A new liberal world order, where the very concept of the State will make less and less sense.

The world we're entering is a world of abundance. AI, robots, energy, space. And that abundance won't come through the State, for one simple reason: we have a century of proof that it doesn't work.

Redistribution was version 1.0. Direct distribution of capital is 2.0.

While France is still debating how to tax builders even more, America is handing stock to its kids.

Pick your side.
